passage: For the Class 10 farewell at the government school in the kasba, Saurabh listed every cost on the back of a notebook page: samosas, tea, a banner, decorations. Total: 2,400 rupees. With thirty classmates that came to eighty each, but Rashmi, who kept the class money box, said, "Some can't give eighty. Make it fifty." So Saurabh went back to the list. Shop samosas cost nine hundred, but if mothers made pakoras at home, three hundred. The art club could paint the banner. Rashmi drew a big sheet on chart paper and pinned it to the classroom wall: every name, every payment, every purchase. By Friday it showed 1,420 collected and 1,180 spent. "Left: 240," Rashmi wrote, "for the tea."

qa.q: How much was each classmate asked to give in the end?
qa.a: Each classmate was asked to give fifty.

qa.q: Why did Rashmi want the limit lowered, and how did Saurabh respond?
qa.a: Rashmi worried that some classmates could not afford eighty, and Saurabh accepted it and went back to the list to find cheaper options.

qa.q: What else could Saurabh do if collections run short, and why?
qa.a: Saurabh could cut the decorations or ask a shopkeeper for a small donation of tea leaves, because the shared sheet shows exactly where money can be saved.

qa.q: How might a classmate who cannot afford much see the fifty rupee limit?
qa.a: That classmate would likely feel relieved and included, since the party stays affordable and everything is written openly on the wall.

grounding: The organiser lists all expected costs, sets what each classmate can contribute, prices alternatives such as home-made snacks, and tracks spending on a shared sheet.
